verdicts.quote: The time went so quickly that we missed the last bus.
verdicts.reason: This is not a natural use of uncountable time; say “Time went by so quickly” or “The time passed so quickly.”
This sense is normally countable in “a good time”, “the time”, and “it is time”; uncountable uses belong to other senses.

verdicts.quote: After the first time and the last time English uses the present perfect
verdicts.reason: This is overgeneralized: “the last time” can take a simple past when it refers to a completed past occasion, as in “The last time I saw her, she was ill.”

verdicts.quote: the regular pattern of beats in a piece of music, and how fast they come
verdicts.reason: It conflates musical time with tempo; time is the metrical pattern of beats, while tempo is the speed.
This falsely treats timetable and schedule as regional equivalents; timetable is used in American English too, though schedule is often more common.

verdicts.quote: "It's the first time I visit this city." / "It's the first time I have visited this city."
verdicts.reason: The correction is valid, but the learner error is less clear in American English, where “It is my first time visiting this city” is also standard.

verdicts.quote: English uses one word where many languages use three
verdicts.reason: The adaptation note is not language-neutral because it makes a broad and unsupported claim about many languages.

verdicts.quote: In English-speaking countries clock times are usually given with the twelve-hour clock, seven in the evening rather than nineteen hundred
verdicts.reason: This is an overgeneralization: twenty-four-hour time is also common in timetables, transport, military, medical, and other formal contexts.

verdicts.quote: In many languages the word for time also means weather; English time never does.
verdicts.reason: This is a broad unsupported cross-linguistic claim and is not language-neutral.
